title: Branching strategies: feature, main, release

overview.what:
A branching strategy is a set of rules a team follows for organizing their Git branches. The most common branches are `main`, feature branches, and release branches.

Imagine a large Google Doc that 10 people are editing. Instead of everyone typing over each other, each person gets a private copy (a feature branch). When they finish, their copy is reviewed and carefully merged into the master copy (the `main` branch).

- `main` — The master copy. This code is always stable and ready for users.
- `feature/login` — A temporary branch created by one developer to build the login page. It branches off `main`.
- `release/v1.0` — A branch created right before launch to freeze the code and fix final bugs.

The rule is: **never write code directly on the `main` branch.** You always create a feature branch, do your work there, and merge it back only when it is finished and tested.
overview.why: It keeps the main codebase stable. If your new feature breaks completely, the main project is safe because your broken code is isolated on your feature branch.

why_learning_this: You will not accidentally break the code that thousands of users are relying on.
You can work on your own features peacefully without teammates overwriting your changes.

common_mistakes.title: Committing directly to main
common_mistakes.explanation: You forget to create a new branch and write all your code on `main`. If it has a bug, the live product immediately breaks.

common_mistakes.title: Keeping a feature branch alive too long
common_mistakes.explanation: You work on a feature branch for two months without merging. By the time you try to merge, `main` has changed completely, causing massive merge conflicts.

recall_questions.q: Explain the purpose of a feature branch in your own words, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: It is a private copy of the code where a developer can build a new feature without breaking the stable main codebase.

recall_questions.q: Why is it dangerous to write code directly on the 'main' branch?
recall_questions.answer: Because the main branch holds the stable, live code. Any bug you write there will immediately affect the final product.

understanding_checks.question: You are building a shopping cart. Halfway through, the boss asks you to quickly fix a typo on the homepage. Should you fix it on your shopping cart branch?
understanding_checks.answer: No. You should switch back to main, create a new branch just for the typo fix, merge that, and then return to your shopping cart branch.
understanding_checks.why: Never write code directly on the main branch, and keep feature branches focused on one task. Mixing a typo fix with an unfinished feature means the typo won't be fixed live until the cart is fully done.

understanding_checks.question: A teammate says, 'I created a release branch for version 2.0, so I will start building all the version 3.0 features on this release branch.' What is wrong with this?
understanding_checks.answer: Release branches are strictly for final bug fixes before launch, not for building new features.
understanding_checks.why: A release branch freezes the code for a specific launch. New features should always go on new feature branches that branch off main.

code_walkthrough.code:
def git_workflow_simulator():
    main_branch = ['stable code']
    feature_branch = main_branch.copy()
    
    feature_branch.append('new login feature')
    # feature is tested, now merge:
    main_branch = feature_branch.copy()
    print('Main now has:', main_branch)

git_workflow_simulator()

aha_moment.prediction: In this analogy, if you break your feature branch, does the main branch break too?
aha_moment.why: No, because a branch is a completely isolated copy. Breaking your feature branch leaves the main branch completely safe.
